messages.subject: rstanarm for survey data
parts:
Hi,

I would like to use rstanarm rstan for fitting models to survey data and important thing is that I need to use sampling weights. The weights are represented as simple vectors between {0;1} as a column in a dataframe. Is it possible to apply these weights with rstanarm? And if not, is this possible with rstan?

Thanks and Cheers,
Carsten

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: rstanarm for survey data
parts:
On Friday, May 20, 2016 at 11:26:49 AM UTC-4, Carsten Schwemmer wrote:
I would like to use rstanarm rstan for fitting models to survey data and important thing is that I need to use sampling weights. The weights are represented as simple vectors between {0;1} as a column in a dataframe. Is it possible to apply these weights with rstanarm? And if not, is this possible with rstan?

The model-fitting functions in rstanarm take a (almost entirely untested) weights argument. However, utilizing them is essentially un-Bayesian. For model-based approaches, I think it is better to get the posterior distribution of the parameters conditional on the (unweighted) data in the sample and then obtain posterior predictions for the population that the sample was taken from. The posterior_predict() function in rstanarm facilitates this and a similar thing is done by mrp

https://github.com/malecki/mrp

Ben

messages.author: 1457d345496c6c07
messages.subject: Re: rstanarm for survey data
parts:
Hi Carsten,
This is a subject I am very close to. I've posted a couple of Rpubs documents on how I implement suggestions from the literature:
http://rpubs.com/corey_sparks/164805
http://rpubs.com/corey_sparks/157901

And by literature, I'm speaking of ch 14 of Snijders and Bosker's text "Multilevel Modeling 2nd edition", as well as Rabe-Hesketh and Skrondal (2006)  and  Carle (2009) 

which provide several techniques for using design weights when using multilevel regression models. The implementation in brms() weights the likelihood function, and I believe rstanarm probably does it the same way. 
-Corey

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: rstanarm for survey data
parts:
Yes, you weight the likelihood.

If you have weight w[i] for item i, then a simple linear
regression of y on x would be this in Stan:

increment_log_prob(w[i] * normal_log(y[i], alpha + beta * x[i], sigma));

- Bob

Many thanks for your replies :)

I will have a look at the docs as well as the literature Corey provided. There is  one thing that I don't really understand (I'm just getting started with Bayesian Modeling): What does Ben mean with using weights being "un-Bayesians"?

To me, weights are un-Bayesian because the violate the likelihood principle. To others, weights are un-Bayesian because there is no generative model. There is an inconclusive thread on this topic here

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/5pJdH72hoM8/GLW_mTeaObAJ

messages.author: 1457d345496c6c07
messages.subject: Re: rstanarm for survey data
parts:
Regarding the "generating model" idea, Snijders and Bosker spend a lot of time comparing the "model based" regression coefficient estimates, which are derived from the hierarchical model with the level 2 units included to model the between-stratum variance,  to the "design based" model coefficients which are derived from a model which weights the likelihood function.  They present a pretty thorough exploratory treatment of influential units (in terms of their weights). From my reading there is not an agreed up standard, and if all else fails, the model based estimates correspond better with the Bayesian framework of modeling. IMO
-Corey

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstanarm for survey data
parts: For an analysis to be Bayesian, it has to use the posterior distribution, p(theta|y) proportional to p(theta) p(y|theta).  In this weighted regression procedure, there is no model p(y|theta).  The procedure uses certain computations that are used in Bayesian analysis--it has some Bayesian elements--but it is not truly a Bayesian analysis because there is no model.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: rstanarm for survey data
parts:
Just to reiterate some of the points made a while ago in this thread, we recommend the fully Bayesian approach. This would be a multilevel model without weights estimated by MCMC, and then you can use the model to study the population of interest via the posterior predictive distribution, i.e. predicting the outcome in the relevant post-stratification cells. With that you can then calculate whatever summaries you want, and you don't need survey weights at any step in the process.

For standard multilevel (G)LMs this can easily be done in rstanarm with stan_(g)lmer() and posterior_predict(). Of course you can also write out the model and predictions in the Stan language yourself if you want.

Hope that helps,

Jonah
